title: Using translations
hookLine: a pun dies in the subtitles; the Granth's first character is a digit no English can carry
tomorrow: so if the English helps, why read the Gurmukhi at all?

lines: THE PUN DIED IN THE SUBTITLES.
cards: A movie character makes a pun, the subtitles translate it, and nobody in the theater laughs. The joke didn't survive the trip. Here's a stranger case.
The very first character in the Guru Granth Sahib isn't a letter. It's a digit: the number one, written in Gurmukhi, joined to the sign for Onkar. Ik Onkar.
Every English translation has to turn that digit into words. So, the puzzle: can an English line hand you what's on the page?

teach.b: Start with the help. In 1909, Max Arthur Macauliffe published The Sikh Religion, with English renderings of the Gurus' hymns, and later translators made their own. For anyone who can't yet read Gurmukhi, they open a door.
This path leans on them too, mostly in paraphrase. Now the puzzle. Macauliffe's English of the Mul Mantar opens with words about there being one God.

teach.h: ONE GOD? ONE CREATOR? THE ONE?
teach.b: Another version says one creator. Another just says the One. None of them is wrong, and none of them is a digit.
The page says one the way a number says it: plain, before any description. Each translator has to choose, and every choice keeps something and drops something. It happens again two words later.
Sat naam: one English reads it as whose name is true, another as truth is the name. Same Gurmukhi, two shades. So here's the answer.
Yes, translations help, a lot. And each is partial, a window on one side of the house.
Read two side by side and the differences show you where the Gurmukhi holds more than either.
Something to tell a friend tonight: the Sikh scripture begins with a number, and no English sentence can quite be a number.

how: Readers who don't yet know Gurmukhi well often use English translations, from Macauliffe's 1909 renderings to later ones, many apps showing the Gurmukhi above with a translation beneath.

games.q: a friend wants to read the Japji in English and asks you which translation is the real one. what's the honest answer?
o: the oldest English, since it's closest in time to the Gurus.
none is the Gurmukhi; each helps and each is partial, so read two side by side.
any one will do, because meaning crosses into English without loss.
games.why: translations help, a lot. but every translator chooses, even for the opening digit. two versions side by side show where the Gurmukhi holds more.

practice: Find the Mul Mantar's opening in two English versions, in an app, a book or online. Look at them side by side and find one word where they differ.
Then let your eyes rest on the Gurmukhi above them, on the digit one, and breathe slowly, letting it be one before it's any word.

wordCard.voice: Using translations: reading the Granth with English renderings, like Macauliffe's of 1909 and later ones, as real help that is always partial. The eleventh word of the year.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Ik Onkar, the numeral one joined to the sign for Onkar; the Granth's first character.

carryVoice: For the road: translations help, and two of them side by side help more than one. Eleven of twenty.
